Warm Up: Sketching a Solution Curve

Sketch an approximate solution to the system of first-order differential equations with the given initial value:

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -0.5x + 1y + 0 \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 0x - 0.5y + 0 \end{cases} \qquad x(0) = -3,\quad y(0) = 3\]
Diagram description: A vector field is displayed on a grid with both axes ranging from \(-4\) to \(4\). The blue arrows at each grid point show the direction \((dx/dt,\, dy/dt)\). In the upper half of the field, arrows tend to point right then curve downward; in the lower-left quadrant arrows point diagonally upward-right. The pattern is consistent with a stable node or spiral at the origin, where solutions decay toward \((0,0)\) as \(t \to \infty\). The initial condition \((-3, 3)\) is in the upper-left quadrant.

Page 4

Predator-Prey Model — Ecology (Setup)

Variables: Let \(x(t)\) denote the prey population and \(y(t)\) denote the predator population at time \(t\) (measured in years). All constants \(a,\, b,\, c,\, d\) are positive.

Lotka–Volterra Equations:

\[\begin{cases} \dot{x} = ax - bxy \\[4pt] \dot{y} = -cy + dxy \end{cases}\]

where:

  • \(ax\) is the natural (exponential) growth rate of prey in the absence of predators — \(a\) is a positive growth rate constant.
  • \(-bxy\) is the “competition term”: prey are removed at a rate proportional to encounters between predators and prey — \(b\) is a positive constant.
  • \(-cy\) is the natural decay of predators in the absence of prey — \(c\) is a positive decay rate.
  • \(dxy\) is the predator growth term from consuming prey — \(d\) is a positive constant.

Page 5

Predator-Prey Model — Phase Portrait

Specific system:

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -6x + 2xy \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 3y - xy \end{cases}\]
Diagram description: A phase plane is shown with \(x\)-axis (prey) from \(-1\) to \(10\) and \(y\)-axis (predator) from \(-1\) to \(10\). A large closed orange orbit is drawn, indicating a periodic (or near-periodic) solution cycling around an interior equilibrium. A red trajectory starts near \((0, 1)\) on the \(y\)-axis, a green trajectory starts near \((8, 0)\) on the \(x\)-axis, and a blue trajectory begins near \((7.5, 0)\). Handwritten annotations identify three points: \((9,0)\), \((0,1)\), and \((7,7)\). The blue arrow near the bottom indicates “\(y\) starts to decrease.” Small blue field arrows throughout indicate the flow direction.

Question posed in class: Which variable in this picture is prey? Which is predator?

  • At \((9,\, 0)\): \(x\) here is the predator.
  • At \((0,\, 1)\): \(y\) here is the prey.
  • Starting point \((7,\, 7)\) is also noted.

Page 6

Predator-Prey Model — Story Starting at \((7, 7)\)

Narrative of the solution trajectory beginning at \((7,\, 7)\):

Initially, the predator population is increasing while the prey population is decreasing. Around a predator population of approximately 8, the system can no longer support so many predators, so the predator population begins to decrease. The predator population will decrease so low that, around a prey level of approximately 1.5, the prey begins to increase again.

This describes the characteristic cyclical oscillation of the Lotka–Volterra system: predator and prey populations chase each other in a closed orbit in the phase plane.

Page 7

Predator-Prey Model — Finding Equilibria

Equilibria of an autonomous system are found by setting \(\dot{x} = 0\) and \(\dot{y} = 0\) simultaneously.

Visually: Equilibria are the points in the phase plane where no arrows appear — where the vector field is the zero vector.

Algebraically: Set \(\dot{x} = 0\) and \(\dot{y} = 0\) and solve the resulting system of equations.

For the Lotka–Volterra system above, one equilibrium is clearly at \((0,\, 0)\) — when both populations are zero, neither grows nor decays. Another (non-trivial) equilibrium exists at an interior point.

Page 8

Predator-Prey Model — Logistic Modification

Limitation of the basic model: Exponential growth for prey is simplistic. A more realistic model uses logistic growth for the prey population.

Lotka–Volterra with logistic prey:

\[\begin{cases} \dot{x}(t) = ax(t) - bxy \\[4pt] \dot{y}(t) = -cy + dxy \end{cases}\]

In the logistic variant, the prey growth term \(ax\) is replaced by a term that limits growth as prey population approaches a carrying capacity, making the model more ecologically realistic.

Page 9

Predator-Prey Model — Logistic Phase Portrait

Diagram description: A phase plane with both axes running from 0 to 11. A vector field of small black arrows fills the plane. Multiple solution curves are drawn in rainbow colors (from blue/green near the center through yellow, orange, red, and gray for outer orbits). The innermost curves form a small tight loop near approximately \((3,\, 3)\), indicating a stable spiral equilibrium. Outer curves form progressively larger loops that are egg-shaped (wider at the right), suggesting the logistic modification breaks the perfect periodicity of the basic Lotka–Volterra model and instead draws trajectories inward toward the stable equilibrium. The outermost gray curves are the largest loops before solutions potentially leave the biologically meaningful region.

Unlike the basic model whose orbits are closed (periodic), the logistic variant produces a stable spiral: all nearby trajectories spiral inward toward the equilibrium, representing a stable coexistence of predator and prey populations.

Page 10

SIR Model — Epidemiology (Setup)

SIR Model: An illness spreads through a population of size \(N\). The population is divided into three subpopulations:

  • \(S(t)\) — Susceptible: individuals who can contract the illness.
  • \(I(t)\) — Infected (Ill): individuals currently ill and capable of spreading the disease.
  • \(R(t)\) — Recovered: individuals who have recovered and are immune.

SIR System of ODEs:

\[\begin{cases} \dot{S} = -aSI \\[4pt] \dot{I} = aSI - bI \\[4pt] \dot{R} = bI \end{cases}\]

where \(a > 0\) is the transmission rate and \(b > 0\) is the recovery rate.

Conservation law: \(S + I + R = N\) (constant), since the total population is fixed. This means \(\dot{S} + \dot{I} + \dot{R} = 0\).

Page 11

SIR Model — Narrative of an Epidemic

Story of a typical epidemic trajectory:

The population starts mostly susceptible with very few ill individuals. As people get sick, the susceptible population \(S\) decreases while the infected population \(I\) increases. This continues until \(S \cdot b \approx 3.5\), at which point the system starts to “run out” of susceptible people to infect, and recovery begins to outpace new infections. The infected population \(I\) then decreases. Both \(S\) and \(I\) tend toward a final equilibrium as the epidemic subsides.

This dynamics is the characteristic arc of an epidemic modeled by the SIR system: a single peak in the infected population followed by decay to zero, with the susceptible population approaching a positive limiting value.

Page 12

SIR Model — Specific Parameters and Phase Portrait

Specific SIR system (with \(S\) on the horizontal axis, \(I\) on the vertical axis):

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dS}{dt} = -0.04\,S\,I \\[8pt] \dfrac{dI}{dt} = 0.04\,S\,I - 0.07\,I \end{cases}\]

Here \(a = 0.04\) (transmission rate) and \(b = 0.07\) (recovery rate).

Diagram description: A phase plane with \(S\) (susceptible) on the horizontal axis (0 to 10) and \(I\) (infected) on the vertical axis (\(-1\) to 10). A vector field of small blue arrows fills the plane; all arrows in the interior point leftward and downward or leftward, consistent with \(S\) always decreasing and \(I\) first increasing then decreasing. A single green solution curve is drawn starting near \((8,\, 1)\) (high susceptible, low infected). It rises sharply upward and to the left as the epidemic grows, reaches a peak infected value near \(I \approx 3.2\) at approximately \(S \approx 1.75\), then curves down and to the left as infection subsides, ending at a point near \((0.5,\, 0)\) on the \(S\)-axis. The horizontal axis is labeled \(S\).

Page 13

Numerical Approximations — Euler’s Method for Systems

Recall: Euler’s method is the numerical analogue of “following tangent lines.”

For a single ODE \(\dot{x} = F(x)\) with step size \(\Delta t\) and initial condition \(x_0\), Euler’s method approximates the next value and then repeats:

\[x_{n+1} = x_n + F(x_n)\,\Delta t\]

For a system of two ODEs, the same idea applies component-wise:

Euler’s Method for Systems: Given

\[\begin{cases} \dot{x} = f(x, y) \\[4pt] \dot{y} = g(x, y) \end{cases}\]

with initial condition \((x_0, y_0)\) and step size \(\Delta t\), the update rules are:

\[x_{n+1} = x_n + f(x_n,\, y_n)\,\Delta t\] \[y_{n+1} = y_n + g(x_n,\, y_n)\,\Delta t\]

Both components are updated simultaneously using the current values \((x_n, y_n)\), and the process repeats.

Page 14

Numerical Approximations — Euler’s Method (Diagram)

Diagram description: This page contains a diagram illustrating the geometry of Euler’s method applied to a system. A solution curve is drawn in the phase plane. At a current point \((x_n, y_n)\), the vector field arrow gives the direction of travel. Euler’s method follows that arrow for one step of length \(\Delta t\), arriving at \((x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\). The diagram shows the tangent vector at the current point and the straight-line step used to approximate the true curved trajectory. The discrepancy between the straight-line step and the actual curve illustrates the local truncation error of the method.

Page 15

Numerical Approximations — Euler’s Method Update Formulas

The full update scheme for Euler’s method applied to a two-dimensional autonomous system is summarized as follows.

Euler’s Method (System Update):

\[x_{n+1} = x_n + f(x_n,\, y_n)\,\Delta t\] \[y_{n+1} = y_n + g(x_n,\, y_n)\,\Delta t\]

where \(f(x, y) = \dot{x}\) and \(g(x, y) = \dot{y}\) are the right-hand sides of the system. Starting from the initial condition \((x_0, y_0)\), each iteration produces the next approximate state \((x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\).

Both components are updated using the current step’s values before moving to the next step. Smaller step sizes \(\Delta t\) yield more accurate approximations at the cost of more computation.
